params.body:
Another one of mine from #731, found by reading the limiter before Shane tests on his own account.

The `two-factor` limiter allows five requests a minute per user, and I put it on the GET of the mail challenge too, reasoning that opening the page makes a mail leave. The effect is not what that reasoning promises. A wrong code costs two of those five: the POST, and the redirect back to the page. After two mistyped codes the third answers 429, and not only the submission but the challenge page itself. Someone with fat fingers on a phone then stares at "Too Many Requests" for a minute instead of at the field. Measured: GET 200, GET 200, then POST 429 and GET 429. The challenge by app gives five tries, because its page was never counted.

The reasoning was also wrong on its own terms. What bounds the mails is the rem inside `EmailSecondFactor`, one per minute per user. That is stricter than the limiter, and a page load cannot spend it, because it hangs on the code and not on the route. The throttle on the GET added no protection and did take attempts away.

The page is no longer behind it. Both POSTs keep theirs, because those are the guesses.

`R P2-3.23` extended, with the limiter cited for its number; finding `een-paginaverversing-kost-een-poging`, resolved here. `APageLoadIsNotACodeAttemptTest`: four wrong codes in a row and the page keeps answering, and ten page loads send one mail. Verified to bite by putting the throttle back, which fails both.

Nobody has the code by mail switched on yet, so this changes nothing for anyone today.

Full suite green, PHPStan clean.
params.title: A page load is not a code attempt
